extracted.intended_audience: mathematics lecturers, instructors, students, and practicing mathematicians interested in exposition and teaching
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and philosophical notes on lecturing, mathematical exposition, and what mathematicians value (types of mathematicians, mathematical beauty, and career etiquette). Aimed at improving lectures and understanding mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every lecture should make only one main point
rubrics_metrics.description: Every lecture should state one main point and repeat it over and over, like a theme with variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An audience is like a herd of cows; making one main point gives the best chance the audience will move in the intended direction. If several points are made the audience will 'scatter' and lose the thread; they may lose interest and revert to their prior thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never run overtime
rubrics_metrics.description: Running overtime is the one unforgivable error a lecturer can make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After fifty minutes everyone's attention turns elsewhere; even one minute of overtime can destroy the best of lectures. Plan talks to finish within allotted time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give them something to take home
rubrics_metrics.description: Include some memorable item — a joke, anecdote, quirk, side remark, or even a mistake — that attendees will remember after they forget the technical material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many former students forget the course material but recall small memorable moments. Such takeaways help a lecturer be remembered and create lasting impact beyond technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure the blackboard is spotless
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a spotless blackboard to subtly convey the impression that the lecture will be equally spotless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erasing uniformly avoids distracting whirls left on the board. Presentation cleanliness affects audience perception of the talk's quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for old age (career etiquette)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that after a certain age you may be viewed as an institution rather than an individual and adapt to the new role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleagues will excuse mediocre papers ('What did you expect, at his age?') or treat interesting late work as expected; the sensible response is to enjoy and play the role of an institution rather than fight it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never compare fields
rubrics_metrics.description: When talking to outsiders, have nothing but praise for colleagues in all fields; public displays of disunity harm mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid denigrating other areas (even your own field's rivals). Public criticism between fields undermines the well-being of the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember everyday things can be mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances such as the grocery bill, a computer program, and class field theory are all pieces of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss 'Mickey Mouse math' as not real mathematics; recognize and value diverse manifestations and applications of mathematical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not look down on good teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect colleagues who are successful at teaching undergraduate courses; they deserve thanks and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching generates much of the discipline's income and goodwill (e.g., donors remember good teachers). Looking down on good teachers is counterproductive professionally and institutionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic exposition is indispensable
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical theory begins with definitions and derives results from clearly agreed-upon rules of inference; every fact must be put into an axiomatic theory and formally proved if it is to be accepted as true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mathematical facts cannot be experimentally verified like physical facts, axiomatic exposition and formal proof are necessary for acceptance of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics lives as facts and as proofs (two lives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics has two 'lives': one dealing with facts (statements discovered like scientific facts) and another dealing with proofs (axiomatic derivation from definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both concepts are seen in mathematical development: the 'fact' view treats theorems as discoveries; the 'proof' view emphasizes formal derivation and axiomatic frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mathematician's ideal of truth is triviality
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of simplification that whittles complex proofs down to concise arguments supports the notion that theorems are creations of intellect; every theorem is eventually proved trivial and mathematicians idealize triviality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians work to show early difficulties were shortcomings of understanding and to reduce results to analytic trivialities; trivialization is valued as the endpoint of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of mathematicians: problem solver vs theorizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians can be subdivided into problem solvers (value first correct solutions; view exposition as inferior) and theorizers (value theory that trivializes problems; value definitions over individual theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most mathematicians are mixtures, but extremes exist: problem solvers like challenges and mistrust generalizations; theorizers seek general definitions and tolerate theorems as support for definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose mathematician type according to task
rubrics_metrics.description: For practical engineering tasks (e.g., sending a rocket into space) choose a problem solver; for broad education (e.g., teaching a child) prefer a theorizer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the mathematician's strengths to the intended role: problem solvers excel at solving concrete obstacles, theorizers at providing conceptual frameworks and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical beauty is tied to enlightenment and admits degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical beauty is the expression mathematicians use to acknowledge 'enlightenment', which admits degrees and is not easily formalized; beauty is often associated with shortness but frequently requires extensive background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake the 'light bulb' instantaneous-flash model as the norm; teaching should not demand a flash of understanding for every argument. Enlightenment is gradual, requires background, and appreciation often follows understanding of previous clumsy proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rota's writing style: provoke and entertain while challenging
rubrics_metrics.description: Rota 'loves contradiction. He loves to shock. He loves to simultaneously entertain you and make you uncomfortable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His essays deliberately use surprising, contradictory arguments and bold statements to challenge preconceptions; when writing or presenting, consider using provocative elements to engage and unsettle assumptions (with care).
